title: The darkest psalm (Psalm 88)
hookLine: a psalm that ends in darkness, and it's still in the Bible

cards: Open a Bible to Psalm 88, and read the last line first. "Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness." That's the end.
No turn. No but I will trust in thee. No hallelujah tacked on at the bottom.

The psalm stops in the dark, like a phone call cut off mid-sentence. And it isn't tucked away in a footnote. It sits in the songbook among the psalms of praise, read and sung and copied with the rest.

teach.b: Start at the top: "O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee." Whoever prays this is in the dark, but still talking to someone. That thread holds the whole psalm together.

In the middle, the singer feels close to the grave, counted among the dead, forgotten, and throws questions straight at God: "Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?"
And: "LORD, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?" No answer comes inside the psalm. Then the ending.
Other lament psalms turn near the end, as Psalm 13 did back on day one hundred five: but I have trusted, I will sing. This one doesn't.

The heading names Heman the Ezrahite, and darkness is the last word, lover and friend gone. So why is it in the Bible? Jewish and Christian communities kept it and prayed it with the rest of the psalms.

Some readers say that's the point: the Bible makes room for a prayer with no happy ending. Someone in long grief, in depression, awake in the small hours, can find their own words already here, already counted as prayer.

teach.h: WHY IT'S STILL IN THE BOOK.
teach.b: Other readers notice that you don't keep crying day and night to someone you think isn't there. For them, the cry is itself a kind of trust. Not fixed first, not tidied: prayed, as it is.
If the dark is heavy on you, tell someone you trust; and if you ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

how: Some Christians pray Psalm 88 in times of grief or depression, and churches that pray the psalms in order, in daily offices, say it along with the others; some pastors point people to it as permission to pray honestly in the dark.

games.q: you're writing a song from the dark. you've cried day and night. no answer has come. it's time for the last line. how do you end it?
o: turn to praise: but I will trust.
end in darkness, still addressed to God.
stop, and tear the page up.
games.why: Psalm 88 ends "mine acquaintance into darkness," still spoken to God, and the song was kept and prayed with the rest.

practice: Let something still dark come to mind, a loss not healed, a question not answered, a fear that hasn't left, and say it silently as it is, with no silver lining, letting it end where it ends.
If you pray, you can say it to God the way Psalm 88 does, even if the last word is darkness; if you don't, say it to the quiet, and rest in the plain fact that it's been said.

wordCard.voice: The darkest psalm. Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in darkness, and was kept and prayed all the same.

orig.note: Hebrew: a word in the psalm's heading ("Maschil" in the King James Bible). its exact meaning is uncertain.

carryVoice: Your line: even darkness can be prayed. Nothing has to be tidied up first. Go gently.
